2.0.0.en: 1 The mace is lifted up against thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily. 2 For the LORD restoreth the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches. 3 The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. 4 The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings. 5 He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared.

2.0.1.en: The mace is lifted up against thy face.

2.0.6.en: God used Assyria as a rod of discipline for His people, but Assyria exalted itself against God and reproached Him, and used every means to practice savagery against the people of God who were under discipline. Now God sends Babylon as the hammer of the whole earth (Jer 50:23), which begins its blows upon great Nineveh openly and boldly.

2.0.7.en: He calls Babylon: "The mace is lifted up against thy face" [1], and some translate it: "He that crusheth is come up against thy face." Babylon is the axe that God uses to crush Assyria. "Thou art my battle axe and weapons of war: for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms; and with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider; and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider; with thee also will I break in pieces man and woman; and with thee will I break in pieces old man and young; and with thee will I break in pieces the young man and the maid; I will also break in pieces with thee the shepherd and his flock; and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman and his yoke of oxen; and with thee will I break in pieces governors and the wreckage" (Jer 51:20-23).

2.0.8.en: Thus God permitted the army of the Medes and Babylon to destroy Nineveh.

2.0.9.en: On the surface it is a war between states and peoples, but in reality it is God's permission, in support of those who trust in Him and who are under discipline, and for the punishment of arrogant Nineveh. Therefore He announced to Assyria beforehand that Nineveh would be openly shattered, and that every effort to defend it would be in vain. Let Assyria put forth all its efforts to preserve Nineveh, but the decree has gone out from heaven for its destruction. Therefore he says: "Keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily," for all this will profit nothing. Let it station forces to guard its fortresses, and set watchmen in the towers to follow the enemy's attack, and let it encourage its soldiers and multiply its military resources, but let it know: "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:30). In vain does it try to enjoy victory while it resists the Lord Himself.

2.1.0.en: For the LORD restoreth the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches. [2]

2.1.1.en: The prophet declares the reason for the destructive war against Nineveh, which is that Assyria despoiled Jacob, having mistreated the captives from Israel and carried out barbarous attacks on Judah, and stood reproaching the Lord of hosts as unable to save them from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria. As they plundered they are plundered, and as they reproached the Lord of hosts shame comes upon them, and the Lord restores to His people their dignity after disciplining them.

2.1.2.en: In the Septuagint it says: "One has arisen who breathes upon thy face, delivering thee from trial" (Nah 2:2) LXX. Theodoret of Cyrus sees that this offers a kind of breathing for the salvation of man. For He had earlier breathed into Adam the breath of life (Gen 2:7); and since man lost the effect of this divine breath, the Lord Christ came to renew the image of man and to restore it in the holy Apostles, and in all the rest of the believers through the Apostles; He breathed on the face of His disciples, saying: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost" (Jn 20:12). God shattered the Assyrians with the breath of His mouth to save His people; as a type of the work of the Lord Christ, who shatters the tyrant devil with the breath of His Holy Spirit, whom He gave to His Church.

2.1.3.en: The shield of his mighty men is made red.

2.1.4.en: The valiant men are in scarlet.

2.1.5.en: The chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation.

2.2.0.en: And the fir trees shall be terribly shaken. [3]

2.2.1.en: Here he describes the commanders of the army of the Medes and Babylon who attack Nineveh.

2.2.2.en: "The shield of his mighty men is made red": the ancients preferred the color red for the shield; on one side, like those who raise the red flag to terrify the enemy, just like bullfighters who think they provoke the bulls with red flags. On the other side, if one is wounded and his blood is scattered on his shield, the enemy does not notice this, and so is encouraged to fight. Some see that the shields of the Assyrians were of copper, as appears from their antiquities, so that the red color of the shields of the army of the Medes and Babylon was the result of the reflection of the sun's rays on them.

2.2.3.en: "The valiant men are in scarlet," for their garments were scarlet. Xenophon says that the Medes were fond of the color red. Since scarlet is costly, it shows the wealth of the army and its capabilities.

2.2.4.en: "The chariots shall be with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation": a picture of the intensity of the attack, as the enemy's chariots move in a frenzied manner, and sparks fly like fire produced by the friction of the chariot wheels against the stones, so that the wheels are like torches from which rays of fire shoot forth.

2.2.5.en: Perhaps he also means that the enemy's chariots carry fiery torches so that they may carry on the battle by night and by day, for the war does not stop until Nineveh is completely destroyed. The soldiers of Gideon carried lamps in pitchers (Judg 7:16) to guide them and to spread terror among their enemies.

2.2.6.en: This is what God permitted at the appointed time, or in the day of his preparation, so that Nineveh might receive the fruit of its deeds.

2.2.7.en: "And the fir trees shall be terribly shaken": the enemy's army is like towering cypresses, shaking continually to terrify Assyria. Perhaps he wishes to express how fiercely the army moves, as the cypress trees shake with the ground under the feet of the soldiers because of their multitude and their constant powerful movement.

2.2.8.en: The chariots shall rage in the streets.

2.2.9.en: They shall justle one against another in the broad ways.

2.3.0.en: They shall run like the lightnings. [4]

2.3.1.en: It shows the capability of the swift-moving, new military chariots; they are shining, appearing as fiery torches and burning lamps among the trees that surround the roads, because of the reflection of the sun on them. They move with force like lightning, as in a state of frenzy.

2.3.3.en: They shall stumble in their walk.

2.4.0.en: They shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared. [5]

2.4.1.en: Some see that the speech here concerns the king of Assyria, who counts the commanders and heroes of his army and brings the valiant among them to lead the situation in the defense of Nineveh, but they stumble in their walk, and all their efforts fail. Others see that the speech here concerns Nebuchadnezzar, who reminds the commanders of his army, the heroes, not to draw back however strong the fortresses of Nineveh may be. As they hasten toward its wall they stumble, but they do not despair; rather they dig trenches to protect them from the arrows of those besieged inside Nineveh. And they complete the siege with the utmost speed.

2.5.0.en: 6 The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. 7 And Huzzab is discovered, she is brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. 8 And Nineveh is of old like a pool of water: but now they flee away. "Stand, stand!" but none looketh back. 9 Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture. 10 She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather redness. 11 Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid?

2.6.0.en: The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved. [6]

2.6.1.en: The gates of Nineveh were open on the river Tigris, on which the city was built. The wall on the side of the Tigris, on the western side of Nineveh, was 4,530 yards long. On the south, north, and east there were huge water moats that could easily be filled with water from the Khosru; the people of Nineveh filled all the moats and channels with water to surround the city on every side, so that the enemy could not cross over to them with their chariots and horses. Diodorus says that in the third year of the siege, when a great flood occurred, 20 furlongs (4,400 yards) of the walls of Nineveh collapsed, and the king burned himself, his palace, his concubines, and his wealth, and the enemy entered through the breached wall. Thus the prophecy of the prophet Micah was fulfilled: "The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved" [6]; for the heart of the king and those with him in the palace melted from fear, and they resorted to suicide by fire.

2.6.2.en: In the Septuagint it says: "The mountains have fallen" (Nah 2:6) LXX. St. Ambrose sees that the mountains point to the great things by which man is puffed up and exalts himself against God. For whoever has faith as a grain of mustard seed says to the mountain that it be cast into the sea, and it is cast (Mt 17:20).

2.7.0.en: And her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts. [7]

2.7.1.en: Huzzab is the name of the queen of Nineveh who fled from the fire, since it was recorded of the king alone that he was burned with fire. The queen was brought before the enemy and he led her away captive in shame and disgrace, and her maids bewailed her state. Some see that "Huzzab" is a symbol of the city of Nineveh itself.

2.7.2.en: The maids have nothing before them but continual lamentation like the unceasing cooing of doves, and beating on their breasts as a sign of intense grief and of inability to act.

2.7.3.en: And Nineveh is of old like a pool of water, but now they flee away.

2.8.1.en: Nineveh was crowded with inhabitants like a pool full of water (Isa 8:7; Jer 51:13; Rev 17:15), but all are unable to act; rather they are fleeing, and some commanders try to rouse the spirit of courage in them, crying out, saying: "Stand, stand," but none looks back, for they have lost all hope of salvation, and so they flee in every direction without restraint.

2.8.2.en: Take ye the spoil of silver.

2.9.0.en: Take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture. [9]

2.9.1.en: Nineveh gathered its wealth of gold, silver, and precious treasures from the annual tribute, from spoils, and from its huge trade (Nah 3:16; Ezek 27:23-24).

2.9.2.en: The king burned his palace with all the treasures in it, but the enemy took possession of the gold, silver, and treasures of the city and of its great men.

2.9.3.en: She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins.

2.10.0.en: And the faces of them all gather redness. [10]

2.10.1.en: A bitter picture of what Nineveh comes to in ruin and terror. The rich city has become emptiness, even void and waste. And she who dominated many nations has a fainting heart and loosened knees, and cannot stand or flee. The faces of her soldiers and people turn red, as though inflamed with the fire of bitterness and grief. Some translate it: "and the faces of them all are pale."

2.10.2.en: Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions?

2.11.0.en: Where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid? [11]

2.11.1.en: The Assyrian monuments were often adorned with images of lions in various forms, among them the winged lion with a human head.

2.11.2.en: Nineveh, as the capital of the greatest state at that time, was reckoned the dwelling of the lions and the feedingplace of the cubs, where the king and queen walked as a lion and lioness in a forest. Now the surrounding nations stand asking: Where is great Nineveh with her might? Where are her lions, the mighty men of war and her great men? She was like a lions' den full of spoils coming from all the nations subject to her! Assyria tyrannized and plundered for the sake of its capital. Now the capital loses everything, and it is said of her: "The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing" (Ps 34:10).

2.12.0.en: The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin. [12]

2.12.1.en: Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts.

2.13.0.en: And I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard. [13]

2.13.1.en: If the kingdom of Assyria prides itself on its forces and its army that never knew defeat, the One who rises against it is "the Lord of the heavenly hosts," or "the Lord of the forces." It is He who vindicates the oppressed, defends the humiliated, and grants victory to the right.

2.13.2.en: Behold, the chariots of Assyria cannot endure the fires of divine wrath, and they burn from the mere smoke before the flames reach them. This kingdom has no more standing, for its young lions die by the sword, so there is no hope for kings (lions) to rise, nor will it acquire spoils any more, and there are no messengers to send to threaten the nations around it. What Assyria did to the nations is done to it; its deed returns upon its own head (Obad 15).

2.13.3.en: Who will restore my dignity but You?

2.13.4.en: * The enemy robbed me of my inner glory!

2.13.5.en: Instead of heaven, the enemy reigned over my depths.

2.13.6.en: He robbed me of my life and glory, and plundered all my gifts and energies for his own account.

2.13.7.en: This is the dangerous Assyria that humbled my soul.

2.13.8.en: * Behold, Your hand moves to restore the excellency of Jacob!

2.13.9.en: I see Your hands stretched out on the Cross, waiting for the whole world to embrace it with love, and to free it from the devil and all his hosts!

2.13.10.en: * Behold, You lead the battle Yourself, O my God!

2.13.11.en: What enemy can stand before You?

2.13.12.en: Your chariots are mighty and effective, they run like the lightnings.

2.13.13.en: You occupy my heart to give it surpassing victory.

2.13.14.en: You drive the enemy out of it, and take from him all that he seized.

2.13.15.en: He goes out shattered, with no power or strength!

2.13.16.en: * He thought himself a lion, preying with no one to restrain him!

2.13.18.en: His forces were shattered and he fell like lightning from the heaven of our hearts.

2.13.19.en: Glory to You, who give glory to those who trust in You.

3.0.0.en: 1 Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not; 2 The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots. 3 And the horsemen rise up, the flame of the sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of wounded, and a great number of slain; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses.

3.0.2.en: It is all full of lies and robbery.

3.0.3.en: The prey departeth not. [1] 1. The trial of Nineveh begins with the first charge against it, which is that it is a "bloody city." It shed the blood of many innocents, and delighted in torturing captives and cutting off their limbs in a savage manner.

3.0.4.en: * "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity" (Ps 5:5), whether they be slaves or free or an emperor, whoever the worker of iniquity may be. For God reckons persons His friends not on the basis of honors, but on the basis of virtue, as you see.

3.0.5.en: St. John Chrysostom St. Augustine comments on the Psalmist's words: "But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men..." (Ps 55:23), asking us to beware of the murderers of souls more than of those who shed the blood of bodies. [Those who separate themselves from unity kill souls by leading them astray spiritually, not shedding blood bodily].

3.0.6.en: And in his comment on the Psalmist's words: "And shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood" (Ps 106:38), St. Augustine sees that perhaps the Psalmist does not mean here the offering of human sacrifices. Truly this custom existed among many nations, especially in the worship of Baal, where a family would sometimes offer its children as human sacrifices to appease the gods. But what the Psalmist means here is the Israelites' participation in pagan worship and its abominations, so that they bequeathed this crime to their children, who grew up practicing it, and in this way the fathers killed the souls of their sons and daughters, and deprived them of the holy life and of fellowship with God. This killing is more hideous than the killing of the body, for in it there is deprivation of eternal life. 2. The second charge: its use of lying and deceit, for it justified its continual attacks by claiming that it was keeping justice and protecting it, and so it put on a deceptive garment with which it covered its evil intentions. Through lying and deceit the heart is drawn into many evils, for it is not frank with itself so as to live pure and clean, loving God and men, but hides its evils and corruption with deceitful words.

3.0.7.en: * "Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing" (Ps 5:6)... God hates evil, utterly abhors and rejects it. Now the Psalmist calls those who live in evil speakers of lies (of falsehood). Those who have vain aims, who are addicted to pleasures, gluttonous and greedy. Here you see that he reckons all these in the class of liars.

3.0.8.en: He abhors the bloody and deceitful man (Ps 5:6). He points here to the murderer, the schemer of evil, the deceiver, who utters one thing on his lips and carries another in his heart. He who is a wolf in a lamb's garment, there is none worse than he. In other words, while an open enemy can be confronted, the one who hides his evil while actually practicing it is not easily discovered, and so he commits many crimes; therefore Christ warns us of the coming of such people: "which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves" (Mt 7:15).

3.0.9.en: St. John Chrysostom 3. The third charge is robbery and plunder, for they did not cease to steal what belongs to others, and without being satisfied they seek to rob those they prey on. The Psalmist Solomon says: "He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight" (Ps 72:14).

3.0.10.en: * Let us lament with Nahum, and say with him: [Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness] (see Jer 22:13; Nah 3:1). Rather, let us grieve over them as Christ did in His days when He said: [Woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your reward and your consolation] (see Lk 6:24). I ask: "Let us not cease to grieve in this way, and if the matter is unseemly, let us lament over the lukewarmness of our brethren. Let us not weep with a loud voice over one who has actually died, but lament over the thief, the covetous, the miser, and the greedy."

3.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots [2]

3.1.1.en: The prophet takes us into the midst of the battle to hear the sound of the whips with which the drivers of the war chariots urge the horses to hurry, and the sounds of the wheels of the exceedingly swift chariots, the leaping of the horses, and the jumping of the chariots.

3.1.2.en: And the horsemen rise up, the flame of the sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of wounded, and a great number of slain; and there is none end of their corpses.

3.2.1.en: He continues his picture of the battle, for the horsemen rise up to fight so as to leap upon their horses to kill the enemies, and the gleaming swords flash like flame, and the spears aimed at the people of Nineveh glitter. Many are wounded, and the slain are without number; there is no one to gather the corpses, nor does anyone care, but the warriors stumble over them because of their abundance and the flood of blood flowing from them.

3.3.0.en: 4 Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. 5 "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. 6 And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. 7 And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"

3.3.1.en: Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts. [4]

3.3.2.en: She did not take warning from what happened to her army when the angel of the Lord killed 185 thousand in one night, and therefore this happens in Nineveh on the day of her utter ruin. 4. The fourth charge is harlotry. Earlier he pictured Nineveh as the lion that is torn apart and whose cubs hunger and are scattered; here he pictures her as a lewd harlot who urges the nations to pagan worship and its abominations. She prides herself on her beauty and her power to seduce. She destroyed the nations by her harlotry.

3.3.3.en: * Reproof is a rebuking discipline, and the divine Teacher used it in Jeremiah, saying: "Thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed before all, and thou didst not call me to thy house, I am thy father, and the lord of thy virginity" (see Jer 3:3-4). "Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot in the cup of enchantment" (see Nah 3:4). And with an all-embracing and complete skill, after calling the virgin by the scandalous, shameful name of harlotry, He calls her to return to an honored life by filling her with feelings of shame.

3.3.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria 5. The fifth charge: she is the mistress of witchcrafts, or its lady, selling families through her witchcraft. For all that occupied the kingdom of Assyria was to rule the world and bring all the nations under its feet. It did not stop at using war, plunder, and rapine, but resorted also to witchcraft, as the harlot does with her enchantment, hunting young men by bodily allurement and enslaving them.

3.4.0.en: Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. [5]

3.4.1.en: Nineveh thought herself the beautiful lady of the world who captures the nations by her witchcraft and harlotry, so that all submit to the worship of her gods and practice abominations with her. But since God hates evil, He deals with her as a harlot, and exposes her corruption, so that she is like one stripped of the harlot's garments that attract to corruption. This is also what the prophet Isaiah prophesied of Babylon, which afterward followed the same course as Nineveh: "for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate... uncover thy veil, gather up the train, uncover the leg, pass over the rivers; thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen" (Isa 47:1-3). She loses not only her deceitful beauty and her enchantment, but appears in shame and disgrace, loathsome and ugly. Her tricks are exposed to the nations, her evil plans are uncovered, and her weakness and corruption appear. "And I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame" [5]. All realize that she is neither strong nor the lady of the world as she claimed.

3.5.0.en: And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. [6]

3.5.1.en: That city with which the states longed to ally themselves has become a laughingstock and a joke to all.

3.5.2.en: And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say:

3.5.3.en: Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her?

3.6.0.en: Whence shall I seek comforters for thee? [7]

3.6.1.en: Instead of the nations' taking refuge in her out of fear of her authority, they look at what has befallen her, and flee from her, for she is not fit even to dwell in.

3.6.2.en: From the severity of the complete destruction there is none to bemoan her, for there is no hope of her restoration any more, and there are no comforters, for all gloat over her. Everyone who sees her is terrified at what has befallen her, and his tongue cannot utter a word of comfort.

3.7.s.en: 3. She becomes an example like others:

3.7.0.en: 8 Art thou better than populous No Amon that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? 9 Cush and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers. 10 Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains. 11 Thou also shalt be drunken: thou shalt be hid, thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy.

3.7.1.en: Art thou better than populous No Amon that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? [8]

3.7.2.en: Lest Nineveh think, or those who hear the prophecy think, that it is impossible for it to be fulfilled, the prophet gives an example of a town that was strong and secure, and when it walked in evil and persisted in resisting God, the divine wrath came upon it: it is "No Amon."

3.7.3.en: No Amon: some see that it is Thebes, which bore this name, and is in Upper Egypt, and its meaning is "the portion or possessions of Amon." And Amon is the Egyptian god Jupiter.

3.7.4.en: It appears that King Sargon of Assyria is the one who struck No Amon; and as Assyria triumphed over Thebes in spite of all its powers and resources, so the turn comes to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, to lose its glory and be destroyed by the Babylonians.

3.7.5.en: "That was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea." Thebes lay on both banks of the river Nile, east and west, and huge water channels surrounded it, so it was like one in safety, as Nineveh was, for we saw earlier how waters surrounded it, preventing enemy armies from reaching its walls.

3.7.6.en: In the days of Homer, Thebes was famous for its hundred gates.

3.7.7.en: Its ruins and remaining monuments still measure 27 miles around, and contain within them the famous temples of Luxor and Karnak.

3.7.8.en: By the sea he means here "the river Nile," and to this day it is so called in Upper Egypt.

3.7.9.en: Cush and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite.

3.8.0.en: Put and Lubim were thy helpers. [9]

3.8.1.en: Cush: most often what is meant by it is the region of Yemen, and sometimes what is meant is southern Egypt, that is, Nubia, and also Ethiopia. Cush derived its strength and wealth from trade and military aid. It was a support for No Amon.

3.8.2.en: Put and Lubim: two neighboring kingdoms west of Egypt in North Africa, namely Cyrene and Libya, and Egypt depended on them greatly, and No Amon obtained supplies from them, and so lived securely, like a queen sitting on her throne.

3.9.0.en: Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains. [10]

3.9.1.en: Since No Amon sat in safety, proud of her strength and wealth, supported by many lands in the south and north, and surrounded by waters to protect her from any attacks, she did not expect any fall, and behold, she goes into exile, taken captive. Her pride and her strength betrayed her, and her children were dashed in pieces. They cast lots for her great men, for it was the custom of the victorious commanders, when they took a great city, to seize its great men, and then cast lots for them so as to distribute these great men as slaves to the commanders. Instead of golden chains and the display of pomp and greatness, these became naked, barefoot slaves, bound with iron chains, dragged to their country in shame and disgrace.

3.10.0.en: Thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy. [11]

3.10.1.en: What befell the city of No Amon befalls Nineveh, and from the horror of it her inhabitants become drunk, deranged in mind, drinking from the cup of God's wrath against them. As it was said to Jerusalem: "which hast drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury; thou hast drunken the dregs of the cup of trembling, and wrung them out... Therefore hear now this, thou afflicted, and drunken, but not with wine..." (Isa 51:17, 21). And in the prophet Jeremiah it says: "For thus saith the LORD God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the LORD had sent me" (Jer 25:15-17).

3.10.2.en: Origen has a beautiful comment on the phrase: "Every bottle shall be filled with wine" (Jer 13:12). Every man is like a bottle filled with wine, but there are two kinds of wine: a good wine, which is the wine of the love of God that makes the soul drunk, so that it melts in love for God, and lives contemplating Him, as though it were drunk with this love. This wine is prepared by Wisdom: "Wisdom hath... mingled her wine... Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" (Prov 9:1, 5). But the evil wine that fills the wicked is like the wine of Sodom and Gomorrah: "For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah: their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter: their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps" (Deut 32:32-33). He also sees that God holds in His right hand the cup of our good works to grant us His blessings, and in His left hand a cup to discipline us until we return to Him.

3.10.3.en: And St. Augustine speaks to us of the wine of the love of God, saying: [Have not those whose hearts have been changed become drunk? He says: "all the sinners of the earth drink" (Ps 75:8). But who are those who drink the wine? Sinners drink so that they may no longer remain sinners, but that they may be justified, and not be punished].

3.10.4.en: "Thou shalt be hid" [11], that is, Nineveh hides herself in shame because of the disgrace and fear that have overtaken her, for she is unable to face the enemy; and she seeks a stronghold to protect her, but she has no support.

3.11.0.en: 12 All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. 13 Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women! The gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars. 14 Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln. 15 There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts! 16 Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away. 17 Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are. 18 Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them. 19 There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?

3.11.1.en: All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater. [12]

3.11.2.en: The prophet likens her to fig trees when the firstripe figs appear on them, which, when the wind shakes them, drop all the figs that are on them. So Nineveh will not be able to repel the enemy, but her children fall with great speed to be eaten!

3.11.3.en: Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women.

3.11.4.en: The gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies.

3.12.0.en: The fire shall devour thy bars. [13]

3.12.1.en: Her army will be like women unable to defend themselves, and the gates of the city open to the enemy without resistance, and the fires blaze in her bars.

3.12.2.en: Draw thee waters for the siege.

3.12.4.en: Go into clay, and tread the morter.

3.13.1.en: In mockery he asks Nineveh to store water and provisions for the period of the siege so that she may not die of thirst and hunger. For although the city is built on the river Tigris and waters surround it through the river and the water moats, its army and all its inhabitants are unable to go out and drink from them.

3.13.2.en: He asks her to repair her fortresses, and they rebuild every fortress in it or repair it. But all this goes to nothing, and she is like one in mire, unable to be rid of it.

3.13.3.en: There shall the fire devour thee.

3.13.4.en: The sword shall cut thee off.

3.13.5.en: It shall eat thee up like the cankerworm.

3.13.6.en: Make thyself many as the cankerworm.

3.14.0.en: Make thyself many as the locusts! [15]

3.14.1.en: He calls her not to rely on the multitude of her inhabitants and the men of her army, for they become like the cankerworm and the locusts, destructive insects, which cannot stand before the blazing fire, nor stand before the sword.

3.14.2.en: Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven.

3.15.0.en: The cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away. [16]

3.15.1.en: Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day.

3.16.0.en: But when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are. [17]

3.16.1.en: Because of her geographical location on the river Tigris with water channels around her, she was a huge commercial country, but when wrath comes and the enemy rises against her, she turns from a city crowded with merchants into a field laid waste by locusts too many to count. Her great men become like locusts on a cold day, who, when the sun rises, fly, and do not know where they are going.

3.16.2.en: Perhaps he means that the foreign merchants who came to Nineveh for trade, and had acquired great wealth, when they see the enemy coming take their wealth and flee. These are the ones whom Nineveh thought would support her in her time of distress, but like locusts they soon fly away from her, hoping to find a safe place.

3.16.3.en: And some see that by the fleeing locusts he means here the hired soldiers who guard the walls from outside, for being hirelings they see the enemy coming and flee, and do not know where they are going. As the Lord Christ says: "The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep" (Jn 10:31).

3.16.4.en: Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria.

3.16.5.en: Thy nobles shall dwell in the dust.

3.17.0.en: Thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them. [18]

3.17.1.en: The king of Assyria thought he was under the protection of shepherds and commanders, mighty men of valor, but he was surprised by the prophet awakening him and saying to him: "Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria" [18]. His great men lay down, for they were killed and fell in the streets in the dust, while his people fled to the mountains in terror, and there is none to gather them.

3.17.2.en: There is no healing of thy bruise.

3.18.0.en: All that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually? [19]

3.18.1.en: The prophet closes his speech by picturing the state of Nineveh as one who is broken with none to mend the break, and wounded with no healing for the wound, for there is no return to the building of Nineveh, nor to the rise of the state of Assyria anew. And since she was violent with all the nations that fell under her hand, they began to mock her, clapping their hands, as they see the fruit of her evil and reproach her.

3.18.2.en: Let Nineveh be shattered, and let the new Jerusalem arise in me!

3.18.3.en: * The enemy crept into my heart, and set up a kingdom for himself in me.

3.18.4.en: Drive out the king of Assyria, and make a public example of him by Your Cross.

3.18.5.en: Strip him of his authority, and establish Your Kingdom within me!

3.18.6.en: * Remove from me what the enemy planted in me.

3.18.7.en: It is foreign to my nature which You gave me.

3.18.8.en: Remove all love of injustice, and all lying and deceit, remove from me every evil desire, and all vainglory.

3.18.9.en: Expose me before myself, that I may return to You, O You who are all love and mercy.

3.18.10.en: * I confess to You my weakness and my inability to resist, but You are my stronghold!

3.18.11.en: You are the heavenly Physician who heal my wounds, and mend every break in my bones!

3.18.12.en: * Instead of the wine of sin that robs me of my balance, give me the wine of Your heavenly wisdom, that I may be drunk with Your love, and sing of Your mercies.

3.18.13.en: Let me forget the world and all its allurements, and enjoy the earnest of Your heavens!
